name: Parameterized problem kernel
short: A reduced equivalent instance bounded by the parameter.
body: Kernelization is a polynomial-time reduction of (I,k) to an equivalent instance (I′,k′), with total size bounded by a function of k. A polynomial kernel has a polynomial size bound.
example: For Vertex Cover with budget k, a vertex of degree greater than k must be chosen. Remove it and reduce k by 1; continue with valid reduction rules.
note: Equivalent means preserving the answer under the formal definition. Shrinking an input by an arbitrary heuristic is not enough.

sources.title: What is known about Vertex Cover Kernelization?
sources.publisher: Fellows, Jaffke, Király, Rosamond and Weller

name: Approximate / lossy kernel
short: A small problem with a controlled approximation loss.
body: Lossy kernelization relaxes exact preservation for optimization problems. Solutions to the reduced instance are lifted back with a formally bounded degradation in approximation quality.
example: An α-approximate kernel trades a smaller reduced problem for an explicit factor α in the lifted solution guarantee.
note: This is still a formal parameterized guarantee, not arbitrary data reduction or an optimization heuristic called Kernel Search.

name: Belief-revision kernel
short: A minimal set of beliefs that entails a target.
body: An α-kernel of a belief base is an inclusion-minimal subset that implies α. Kernel contraction removes at least one belief from each such subset to stop deriving α.
example: For B={p, p→q, q}, the q-kernels are {q} and {p,p→q}. Removing only the explicit q leaves the second proof intact.
note: A kernel is inclusion-minimal, not necessarily smallest by cardinality. This has no connection to Lean's trusted checker beyond both occurring in logic.

sources.title: Kernel contraction
sources.publisher: Sven Ove Hansson / Journal of Symbolic Logic

name: Cooperative-game kernel / prekernel
short: Payoff allocations balanced by pairwise bargaining power.
body: Davis and Maschler's kernel is a solution concept for transferable-utility games. It uses each player's maximum surplus against another, with qualifications for individual-rationality boundaries.
example: In a symmetric three-player game where only the grand coalition has value 1, the equal split (⅓,⅓,⅓) balances every pair's maximum surplus.
note: The prekernel enforces equality of pairwise maximum surpluses. The kernel's boundary conditions differ. Neither is the game's core or a digraph vertex kernel.

sources.title: The kernel of a cooperative game

name: Digraph kernel
short: An independent, absorbing set of vertices.
body: A digraph kernel is a vertex set with no arcs between its members, such that every vertex outside it has an outgoing arc to a member.
tex: \forall v\notin K\;\exists k\in K:\ v\to k
example: For the chain a→b→c, {a,c} is a kernel: it is independent, and b points to c. A directed 3-cycle has no kernel.
note: Absorption uses outgoing arcs in this convention. A maximal independent set alone is insufficient in a directed graph.

sources.title: Combinatorial Game Theory Foundations Applied to Digraph Kernels
sources.publisher: Aviezri Fraenkel / Electronic Journal of Combinatorics

name: Discriminating / robust safety kernel
short: States from which safety can be maintained against disturbances.
body: A discriminating kernel strengthens viability by introducing a disturbance or opponent. Safety must be preserved using an appropriate control strategy under the stated information pattern.
example: A robot's safe region shrinks when the model must tolerate an adversarial wind rather than one favorable wind trajectory.
note: Quantifier order, when disturbances are observed, and strategy definitions are essential. Robust-control terminology varies across formulations.

sources.title: The calculation of discriminating kernel
sources.publisher: Advances in Continuous and Discrete Models

name: Kernel Search
short: A selected variable subset used by an optimization heuristic.
body: Kernel Search builds and expands a promising subset of decision variables, solving restricted mixed-integer problems while examining additional variable groups.
example: In portfolio optimization, begin with a small set of promising assets and test further asset groups to improve the feasible portfolio.
note: This is a heuristic. It does not imply an equivalent instance of parameter-bounded size, as formal kernelization does.

sources.title: Kernel Search: An application to the index tracking problem

name: Perfect kernel
short: The perfect part left after removing isolated points.
body: Cantor–Bendixson analysis repeatedly removes isolated points, possibly through transfinite stages. In a Polish-space setting, the remaining perfect part is called the perfect kernel.
tex: X=P\sqcup C,\quad P\text{ perfect},\ C\text{ countable}
example: For the Cantor set together with one isolated point outside it, the perfect kernel is the Cantor set.
note: Perfect means closed with no isolated points. Removing isolated points only once need not reach the perfect kernel.

name: Section kern / core
short: The load region that keeps a section in compression.
body: The kern of a cross-section is the region in which an eccentric compressive force can act without creating tensile stress, within the assumed linear stress model.
example: For eccentricity along one axis of a rectangle, the familiar middle-third condition avoids tension.
note: The standard English term is usually kern, not kernel. It is included as a closely related STEM term; a rectangular section's full two-axis kern is a diamond.

sources.title: On the kern of a general cross section

name: Semigroup kernel
short: The intersection of nonempty two-sided ideals.
body: The kernel of a semigroup is its least nonempty ideal when such an ideal exists; one can define it as the intersection of all nonempty ideals. A nonempty finite semigroup has such an ideal.
example: If a semigroup has an absorbing zero element, {0} is an ideal contained in every nonempty ideal, so it is the kernel.
note: This kernel belongs to the semigroup itself. A semigroup homomorphism's congruence kernel belongs to a map.

name: Squarefree kernel / integer radical
short: The product of distinct prime divisors.
body: A common convention defines the squarefree kernel of n as its radical: the largest squarefree divisor of a positive integer n.
example: 72=2³·3², so rad(72)=2·3=6. By contrast, the squarefree part in 72=m²s is s=2.
note: Terminology varies: some sources use squarefree kernel for the squarefree part instead. Check the explicit formula.

sources.title: Product of distinct prime factors of n

name: Topological set kernel
short: The intersection of all open supersets of a set.
body: Some topology literature calls the saturation of A its kernel: the points that cannot be excluded by any open set containing A.
example: In the Sierpiński space with open sets ∅, {1}, {0,1}, the kernel of {0} is {0,1}.
note: This construction can enlarge A. In a T₁ space it equals A, and it differs from the perfect kernel.

sources.title: Λrs-open sets and Λrs-closed sets in topological spaces

name: Viability kernel
short: Initial states from which some safe evolution exists.
body: Within a constraint set, the viability kernel contains states for which at least one admissible evolution stays in the set for the specified horizon, often forever.
example: For a vehicle near a wall, safety depends on position and velocity: some positions are already unrecoverable if the vehicle is moving too quickly.
note: This is an existence guarantee under a model and control constraints. It does not mean every possible control is safe.

name: Visibility kernel
short: All points that can see the entire shape.
body: The kernel of a polygon or suitable polyhedron consists of points from which every point of the shape is visible along a segment staying inside it.
example: A convex polygon's kernel is the whole polygon. For a simple star-shaped polygon, intersect the interior half-planes of its edges.
note: The kernel can be empty. A CGAL geometry kernel is software machinery, not this visible region.
